steps.en: Diastolic function grades how the left ventricle fills, which is how it reveals raised filling pressure before symptoms appear. No single number does the job, so the guideline algorithm combines mitral inflow, annular tissue velocity, tricuspid velocity and left atrial volume into a vote. The path splits early: a normal ejection fraction uses one branch and a reduced ejection fraction or known myocardial disease uses another. Learn the cut points cold, because they recur in heart failure, hypertension and valve clinics. In mitral stenosis, which is common in India, the algorithm does not apply: the tight valve itself shapes inflow and tissue velocities, so grade the valve, not diastole.
Record mitral inflow at the leaflet tips in the apical four chamber: peak E, peak A, E to A ratio and deceleration time.
Record septal and lateral annular e prime by tissue Doppler and compute the average E over e prime ratio.
Record the peak tricuspid regurgitant velocity by continuous wave from every window.
Measure the indexed left atrial volume by the biplane method of its own lesson.
With normal ejection fraction, count abnormal markers among septal e prime, lateral e prime, average E over e prime, tricuspid velocity and atrial volume.
With reduced ejection fraction, start from E to A ratio and peak E, then use E over e prime, tricuspid velocity and atrial volume to separate normal pressure from raised pressure grades.
Trusting e prime with a calcified annulus. Fix: Annular calcification freezes the ring and drops e prime without true diastolic disease, so inspect the annulus before trusting the vote.
Grading fused inflow during tachycardia. Fix: Sinus tachycardia fuses E and A into one peak, so slow the rate or wait before grading.
Accepting a faint tricuspid envelope. Fix: A faint partial tricuspid envelope underreads velocity and hides pulmonary hypertension, so optimise gain and try all windows.
Applying the algorithm in mitral stenosis. Fix: In mitral stenosis the valve drives inflow and annular motion, so the diastolic algorithm is invalid there.
Septal e prime abnormal. Below 7 cm per s. Source: ASE and EACVI 2016 diastolic function by Nagueh and colleagues, section on annular velocities
Lateral e prime abnormal. Below 10 cm per s. Source: ASE and EACVI 2016 diastolic function by Nagueh and colleagues, section on annular velocities
Average E over e prime abnormal. Above 14. Source: ASE and EACVI 2016 diastolic function by Nagueh and colleagues, section on filling pressures
Tricuspid velocity abnormal. Above 2.8 m per s. Source: ASE and EACVI 2016 diastolic function by Nagueh and colleagues, section on pulmonary pressures
Left atrial volume abnormal. Above 34 ml per sq m. Source: ASE and EACVI 2016 diastolic function by Nagueh and colleagues, section on left atrial volume

Reduced ejection fraction first split. E to A 0.8 or less with E 50 cm per s or less means normal pressure; E to A 2 or more means raised pressure. Source: ASE and EACVI 2016 diastolic function by Nagueh and colleagues, section on grading with systolic dysfunction
Constrictive pericarditis flips the usual e prime pattern with a brisk septal annulus, so check the septal to lateral relationship.
Positive pressure ventilation and loading shifts move E over e prime within hours, so compare studies at matched states.
Dyssynchrony and pacing distort annular velocities, so grade with extra caution there.

remember.en: Name the traps that invalidate the algorithm

q.en: Which septal e prime is abnormal?

why.en: The ASE and EACVI 2016 cut point for abnormal septal annular velocity is below 7 cm per s.

q.en: Which average E over e prime suggests raised filling pressure?

why.en: An average E over e prime above 14 is one of the four markers of diastolic dysfunction and raised left atrial pressure.

q.en: In reduced ejection fraction, which pattern means normal filling pressure?

o.en: E to A 0.8 or less with E 50 cm per s or less
Any E over e prime above 14

why.en: An E to A ratio of 0.8 or less with peak E 50 cm per s or less marks grade one physiology with normal pressure at rest.

q.en: Why does mitral stenosis block the diastolic algorithm?

o.en: Do not apply the algorithm; grade the valve instead

why.en: The stenotic valve itself shapes inflow velocities and annular motion, so the cut points lose meaning and the valve severity grading takes over.
